questions.q:
Suppose $p, q, r \neq 0$ and system of equation
$\begin{gathered}
(p+a) x+b y+c z=0 \\
a x+(q+b) y+c z=0
\end{gathered}a x+b y+(r+c) z=0$, has a non-trivial solution, then the value of $\frac{a}{p}+\frac{b}{q}+\frac{c}{r}$ is
questions.solution:
Let $|A|=\left|\begin{array}{ccc}p+a & b & c \\ a & q+b & c \\ a & b & r+c\end{array}\right|$
Also, given that equations has non trivial solution
$|A|=0\begin{aligned}
& \Rightarrow \quad\left|\begin{array}{ccc}
p+a & b & c \\
a & q+b & c \\
a & b & r+c
\end{array}\right|=0 \\
& \Rightarrow(p+a)[(q+b)(r+c)-b c]-b[a(r+c)-c a] \\
& +c[a b-a(q+b)]=0 \\
& \Rightarrow \quad(p+a)[q r+q c+b r]-b[a r]+c[-a q]=0 \\
& \Rightarrow \quad p q r+p q c+p b r+a q r=0
\end{aligned}$
Dividing whole equation by $p q r\begin{aligned}
\Rightarrow & \frac{p q r}{p q r}+\frac{p q c}{p q r}+\frac{p r b}{p q r}+\frac{q r a}{p q r} & =0 \\
\Rightarrow & 1+\frac{c}{r}+\frac{b}{q}+\frac{a}{p} & =0 \\
\Rightarrow & \frac{a}{p}+\frac{b}{q}+\frac{c}{r} & =-1
\end{aligned}$

questions.q: The equations $x-y+2 z=43 x+y+4 z=6x+y+z=1$ have
questions.solution:
Given equations, $x-y+2 z=43 x+y+4 z=6x+y+z=1$
Let $\Delta=\left|\begin{array}{ccc}1 & -1 & 2 \\ 3 & 1 & 4 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{array}\right|=1(1-4)+1(3-4)+2(3-1)=-3-1+4=0$
and $\Delta_1=\left|\begin{array}{ccc}4 & -1 & 2 \\ 6 & 1 & 4 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{array}\right|=4(1-4)+1(6-4)+2(6-1)=-12+2+10=0$
Now, $\Delta=0$ and $\Delta_1=0\therefore$ These equations have infinitely many solutions.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q:
If the system of linear equations $2 x+y-z=7x-3 y+2 z=1 ; x+4 y+\delta z=k$
where $\delta, k \in \mathbb{R}$ has infinitely many solutions, then $\delta+k$ is equal to:
questions.solution:
For getting infinite solutions $\mathrm{D}=0, \mathrm{D}_1=\mathrm{D}_2=\mathrm{D}=0$ then check all the three equations
Let $\Delta=\left|\begin{array}{ccc}2 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & -3 & 2 \\ 1 & 4 & \delta\end{array}\right|=0 \quad \Rightarrow \delta=-3$
And $\Delta_1=\left|\begin{array}{ccc}7 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & -3 & 2 \\ k & 4 & -3\end{array}\right|=0 \Rightarrow k=6\Rightarrow \delta+k=3$

questions.solution: $Since, the system has no solution. \left|\begin{array}{ccc}2 & -1 & 2 \\ 1 & -2 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & \lambda\end{array}\right|=0\Rightarrow 2(-2 \lambda+1)+1(\lambda+1)+2(3)=0\Rightarrow \quad-4 \lambda+2+\lambda+1+6=0\Rightarrow \quad 3 \lambda=9 \Rightarrow \lambda=3$

questions.solution: As the given system of equations has a non-trivial solution. $\Delta=\left|\begin{array}{lll}p & a & a \\ b & q & b \\ c & c & r\end{array}\right|=0$ Applying $C_2 \rightarrow C_2-C_1$ and $C_3 \rightarrow C_3-C_1\Delta=\left|\begin{array}{ccc}p & a-p & a-p \\ b & q-b & 0 \\ c & 0 & r-c\end{array}\right|=0$ Expanding along $C_3$, we get $(a-p)\left|\begin{array}{cc}b & q-b \\ c & 0\end{array}\right|+(r-c)\left|\begin{array}{cc}p & a-p \\ b & q-b\end{array}\right|=0\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow(a-p)(-c)(q-b)+(r-c) \\ & \{p(q-b)-b(a-p)\}=0 \\ & \Rightarrow \\ & (p-a)(q-b) c+p(r-c)(q-b)+b(r-c)(p-a)=0 \end{aligned}$ Dividing by $(p-a)(q-b)(r-c)$, we get $\frac{c}{r-c}+\frac{p}{p-a}+\frac{b}{q-b}=0\Rightarrow \frac{p}{p-a}+\frac{q}{q-b}+\frac{r}{r-c}=\frac{q-b}{q-b}+\frac{r-c}{r-c}=2$

questions.q: Let $a, b, c \in \mathbbR^{+}$ and the system of equations $( 1 - a ) x + y + z = 0, x + ( 1 - b ) y + z = 0$ and $x + y + ( 1 - c ) z = 0$ has infinitely many solutions, the minimum value of $abc$ is
questions.solution:
We have,

$\left(1 - a\right)x + y + z = 0$

$x + \left(1 - b\right)y + z = 0$

$x + y + \left(1 - c\right)z = 0$

has many solutions~

$∴ \left|\begin{cases}1 - a & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 - b & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 - c\end{cases}\right| = 0$

$⇒ ab + ac + bc = abc$

$∴ \dfrac{ab + bc + ac}{3} \ge \left(a^{2}b^{2}c^{2}\right)1 / 3 ⇒ \left(abc\right)1 / 3 \ge 3$

$∴$~Minimum of $abc = \left(3\right)3 = 27$

questions.q: If $x^{2} = \left|\begin{cases}sin\theta & cos\theta & 0 \\ - cos\theta & sin\theta & 1 \\ sin\theta & cos\theta & 2\end{cases}\right|$ then the value of $4x^{2} + xsin\dfrac{3\pi}{2} + 5$& is
questions.solution:
Given,& $x^{2} = \left|\begin{cases}sin\theta & cos\theta & 0 \\ - cos\theta & sin\theta & 1 \\ sin\theta & cos\theta & 2\end{cases}\right|$

On expanding $\left|\begin{cases}sin\theta & cos\theta & 0 \\ - cos\theta & sin\theta & 1 \\ sin\theta & cos\theta & 2\end{cases}\right|$ along ${C}_{3}$, we get

$x^{2} = 0 - 1\left|\begin{cases}sin\theta & cos\theta \\ sin\theta & cos\theta\end{cases}\right| + 2\left|\begin{cases}sin\theta & cos\theta \\ - cos\theta & sin\theta\end{cases}\right| = - 1 \left($ sin\thetacos$\theta -$ sin\thetacos$\theta\right) +2\left({sin}^{2}\theta + {cos}^{2}\theta\right)

$= - 1 $\times0 + 2 \times1$

$⇒ x^{2} = 2 ⇒ x = $\pm \sqrt{2}

If $ x = \sqrt{2}, then

4x^{2} + xsin\dfrac{3\pi}{2} +5 = 4 \times $\$left(\sqrt{2}\right)$$2 - $$\sqrt{2} +$$5$

$= 8 - $$\sqrt{2} +$$5 = $$\left(13 - \sqrt{2}\right)$

If $x = - $$\sqrt{2},$ then

4x^{2} + xsin\dfrac{3\pi}{2} +5 = 4 \times \left(- \sqrt{2}\right)2 + \sqrt{2} +5$

$= 8 + \sqrt{2} +5 = \left(13 + \sqrt{2}\right)$$

$

questions.q: The determinant $\left|\begin{array}{ccc}1 & (x-3) & (x-3)^{2} \\ 1 & (x-4) & (x-4)^{2} \\ 1 & (x-5) & (x-5)^{2}\end{array}$\right|
questions.solution:
The given determinant vanishes, i.e.,



$\left|\begin{array}{ccc}1 & x-3 & (x-3)^{2} \\

1 & x-4 & (x-4)^{2} \\

1 & x-5 & (x-5)^{2}

\end{array}$\right|=0



Expanding along $\mathrm{C}_{1}$,$ we get



$\begin{array}{l}

(x-4)(x-5)^{2}-(x-5)(x-4)^{2}-$\left\{(x-3)(x-5)^{2}\right. \\

\left.-(x-5)(x-3)^{2}\right\}$+(x-3)(x-4)^{2} \\

-(x-4)(x-3)^{2}=0 \\

\Rightarrow(x-4)(x-5)(x-5-x+4) \\

-(x-3)(x-5)(x-5-x+3) \\

+(x-3)(x-4)(x-4-x+3)=0

\end{array}$



\Rightarrow-(x-4)(x-5)+2(x-3)(x-5)-(x-3)



$(x-4)=0$

\Rightarrow-x^{2}+9 x-20+2 x^{2}-16 x+30-x^{2}+7 x-12=0



$\Rightarrow-32+30=0 \Rightarrow-2=0Which is not possible, hence no value of $\mathrm{x} satisfies the given condition.$

Let \(D=$\left[$\begin{array}{ll}a & b \\ c & d \\ e & f\end{array}$\right]\)
$\begin{aligned}$& \therefore A+B-C=$\left[\begin{array}{ll}1 & 3 \\ 3 & 2 \\ 2 & 5\end{array}$\right]+$\left[\begin{array}{cc}-1 & -2 \\ 0 & 5 \\ 3 & 1\end{array}$\right]-$\left[$\begin{array}{ll}$\mathrm{a}& \mathrm{b}$\\ $\mathrm{c}& \mathrm{d}$\\ $\mathrm{e}& \mathrm{f}\end{array}$\right]$\\ & \Rightarrow $\left[$\begin{array}{ll}1-1-\mathrm{a}$& 3-2-$\mathrm{b}\\ 3+0-\mathrm{c}$& 2+5-$\mathrm{d}\\ 2+3-\mathrm{e}$& 5+1-$\mathrm{f}$\end{array}$\right]=\left[\begin{array}{ll}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{array}$\right]\end{aligned}\)
$\begin{array}{ll}-\mathrm{a}$=$0 \Rightarrow \mathrm{a}$=$0,1-\mathrm{b}$=$0 \Rightarrow \mathrm{b}$=$1, \\ 3-\mathrm{c}$=$0 \Rightarrow \mathrm{c}$=$3, & 7-\mathrm{d}$=$0 \Rightarrow \mathrm{d}$=$7, \\ 5-\mathrm{e}$=$0 \Rightarrow \mathrm{e}$=$5, & 6-\mathrm{f}$=$0 \Rightarrow \mathrm{f}$=$6,\end{array}$

Let \(A\) be the 1 st term and \($\mathrm{R}$\) the common ratio of G.P., then
\$(\begin{aligned} \text{$ and } a=T_p=A R^{p-1} \\ $\text{$ and } \therefore $\log$$\mathrm{a}=\log \mathrm{A}+$($\mathrm{p}-$$1) $$\log$$\mathrm{R}

and \(\log $\mathrm{c}=\log \mathrm{A}+(\mathrm{r}-$1) \log $\mathrm{R}$\)

1 \text{ and } r \text{ and } 1

q-1 \text{ and } q \text{ and } 1 \\
r-1 \text{ and } r \text{ and } 1

Apply \(\mathrm{C}}_{1} \rightarrow \mathrm{C}}_{2} \rightarrow \mathrm{C}}_{3}\) in the second
\$(\Delta=$0+$\log R\left|$$\begin{array}{lll}0 & p & 1 \\
0 & q & 1 \\
